blocks.heading: Barriers and matching remedies
blocks.text: Communication barriers include noise, unfamiliar language or jargon, ambiguous wording, inaccessible channels, poor timing, information overload, long reporting chains and attitudes that discourage listening or honest feedback. Match the remedy to the cause. Move a safety briefing away from loud machinery; use plain language and check meaning where terms are unfamiliar; give dates and responsibilities instead of vague instructions; use a channel the receiver can access. Send information early enough to act and prioritise the essential message instead of burying it in many notices. Shorter communication routes can reduce distortion, while respectful opportunities for questions can reveal hidden misunderstanding. Repeating the same unclear message more loudly does not necessarily solve a language problem. A method is effective in its circumstances, not because it is modern or widely used.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Osa Workshop announces tomorrow’s changed shift time beside a running machine. Several workers hear different times and do not ask because they fear criticism. Pause for a quiet briefing, state the exact day and time, provide an accessible written reminder and invite workers to confirm the arrangement without blame. This addresses noise, ambiguity and fear of feedback rather than assuming a notice sent later will repair tomorrow’s missed start.
